issues.legal_issue: Payment of compensation to avoid further proceedings for a forest offence does not, without an express legal provision, amount to an acquittal or vindicate the payer’s character.
material_facts: The licence holder paid compensation after a forest officer detected that green trees had been illegally felled and converted into firewood.
The forest regulation provided that payment discharged a person in custody, released seized property, and barred further proceedings, but did not provide that payment had the effect of an acquittal.
The Board of Revenue considered the licence holder’s conduct in paying compensation when assessing his suitability for an excise licence.
issues.conclusion: The compensation payment did not have the effect of an acquittal or clear the licence holder’s character; the Board could consider the conduct underlying the payment when assessing suitability.
issues.legal_principle: The effect of a legally permitted composition depends on what the governing law expressly provides. Section 345(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 expressly gives composition of the offences specified in section 345(1) and (2) the effect of an acquittal. Section 62(2) of the Assam Forest Regulation, 1891 only protects against further proceedings and does not confer that effect or vindicate the payer’s conduct. The Court rejected the analogy with section 345(6), and also declined to rely on the observations in Chandanmal v. Rupakula Ramkrishnayya and Reg. v. Rahimat to treat compensation as clearing the person’s character.

predicates.forest_offence_compensation_case: A person suspected of a forest offence paid compensation under a process that permits the offence to be dealt with by payment.
predicates.compensation_paid_to_avoid_further_proce: The person paid compensation to avoid further proceedings in relation to the suspected offence.
predicates.governing_law_does_not_expressly_make_pa: The law governing the payment bars further proceedings but does not say that payment has the effect of an acquittal.

issues.definition: When a person pays compensation to avoid further proceedings for a forest offence and the governing law does not expressly make that payment an acquittal, the payment does not vindicate the person’s character.

issues.legal_issue: A court exercising certiorari jurisdiction cannot quash a licensing authority’s decision where the authority was entitled to consider the applicant’s conduct and did not exceed its jurisdiction or commit an apparent error of law.
material_facts: The Board of Revenue considered the licence holder’s payment of compensation for a forest offence when deciding whether he was suitable to hold an excise licence.
The Board had authority to assess suitability and could treat the applicant’s conduct as relevant to that assessment.
The High Court quashed the Board’s decision on the view that the compensation payment had the effect of an acquittal.
The Supreme Court found that the Board had not exceeded its authority or committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in quashing the Board’s decision by certiorari. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the Board’s order was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, certiorari is not a substitute for an appeal and is available to address an inferior tribunal’s excess of jurisdiction or failure to follow essential legal requirements, including an error of law apparent on the face of the record. The Court applied Nagendra Nath Bora v. The Commissioner of Hills Division and Appeals, Assam, which explains these limits and recognizes that an appellate authority’s powers in licensing settlement may be co-extensive with those of the primary authority.

predicates.certiorari_challenge_to_licensing_settle: A party sought certiorari to quash a decision concerning the settlement of a licence.
predicates.licensing_authority_considered_applicant: The licensing authority considered the applicant’s conduct when assessing suitability for the licence.
predicates.authority_entitled_to_assess_suitability: The authority had power to assess the applicant’s suitability and to consider conduct relevant to that assessment.
predicates.no_jurisdictional_excess_or_apparent_err: The authority acted within its legal powers and its decision did not contain an error of law apparent on the face of the record.

issues.definition: When a licensing decision challenged by certiorari rests on conduct the authority was entitled to consider and the authority neither exceeded its jurisdiction nor made an apparent legal error, the decision is not quashed by certiorari.
